title: Open-Source Infrastructure for Human-Centered AI Auditing
oneLiner: A configurable platform for studies that combine surveys, live chatbot interaction, turn-level annotation, and structured data export.
teaser: A reusable platform for running human-centered AI evaluations with surveys, live chatbot conversations, guided auditing, turn-level annotation, and structured export. I am turning the system used in our 254-participant study into open-source research infrastructure.
summary: Human-centered AI studies often require researchers to rebuild the same components: consent and survey flows, a chat interface, model connections, annotation tools, logging, and data export. I am turning the system used in our 254-participant chatbot study into an open-source platform that can support different models, tasks, and study designs.
problem: The original system was built for one interactive chatbot study. The open-source version separates study content from application logic so researchers can configure a new evaluation without rewriting the platform. It also preserves the link between a conversation turn, a participant's annotation, and the survey measures used in later analysis.
role: I designed and built the platform and continue to lead its open-source development.
built: Configurable survey, chat, audit, and completion flows
Live chatbot interaction through a model-relay server
Turn-level highlighting and annotation of model responses
Likert and free-text responses tied to specific conversation turns
Tutorial gating before the main task
Structured local (IndexedDB) and server-side storage, export, and replay
Study content separated from application logic

headings.problem: From one study to a platform

scale: Used in a study with 254 participants and 551 conversations

title: Lay-User Auditing and Trust in Generative AI
oneLiner: In 551 chatbot conversations, participants often failed to find the problems they expected, while probing generally increased their trust.
teaser: We asked 254 U.S. participants to investigate whether a chatbot produced problematic, questionable, or unfair responses. Across 551 conversations, participants often failed to uncover the issues they expected, and trustworthiness ratings generally rose after the exercise.
pullQuote: Trustworthiness ratings generally increased after probing, whether or not participants detected a problem.
summary: We asked 254 U.S. participants to investigate whether a chatbot produced problematic, questionable, or unfair responses. Using a researcher-supplied probing tool, participants held 551 open-ended conversations and flagged issues they encountered. Participants frequently failed to uncover the problems they expected to find. Trustworthiness perceptions increased after probing whether or not a problem was detected, and participants with higher initial trust were less likely to flag one.
problem: User-driven auditing assumes that people can turn their concerns about AI into evidence through direct interaction. This study tests that assumption by comparing what participants tried to uncover, what they actually flagged, and how the audit exercise changed their perceptions of the chatbot.
whyItMatters: The results suggest that lay users may recognize that generative AI raises concerns without being well equipped to surface those concerns on their own. They also show that an unsuccessful audit can increase confidence rather than calibrate it.
role: I led the implementation and deployment of the interactive study platform and contributed to the study design and analysis with the research team.
findings: Participants frequently failed to uncover the problems they expected to find.
Trustworthiness perceptions increased after probing, whether or not a problem was detected.
Participants with higher initial trust were less likely to flag a problem.
status: Published at FAccT 2026 · related work at SOUPS 2025 and ConPro 2025
collaborators: With co-authors at The George Washington University and partner universities.

title: Reflecting on AI Interaction Histories
oneLiner: A dashboard study of what people notice when months of ChatGPT conversations become reviewable as a single record.
summary: People disclose information to chatbots one conversation at a time, while providers retain the entire history. A conversation that seemed minor when it occurred may later reveal sensitive information, reliance patterns, emotional context, or changes in how someone uses the system. This study asks what people notice when they review their own ChatGPT histories and whether that review changes privacy concern, trust, disclosure awareness, or plans to manage stored conversations.
problem: Most people experience AI histories as separate chats rather than as an accumulated record. The study makes selected parts of that record reviewable and asks whether retrospective reflection reveals risks or benefits that were not apparent during the original interaction.
role: I designed the study and am building the participant-facing dashboard and data-collection system.
built: Consent-based collection of a participant's own ChatGPT history
Participant- and researcher-selected sampling of past conversations
A dashboard for reviewing selected conversations with guided reflection prompts
Pre- and post-review measures of privacy concern, trust, disclosure awareness, and data-management intentions
status: IRB and ethics approvals complete · pilot completed · recruitment pending
statusNote: Results will be reported when the main study is complete.

title: Employee Adoption and Governance of Generative AI
oneLiner: Interviews with NIST employees about where generative AI fits into their work, where they avoid it, and how they judge and verify its outputs.
summary: This study examines the tasks employees use generative AI for, the outcomes and impacts they experience, and the reasons they use or avoid it. Interviews also ask how employees decide that a use is appropriate, how they check generated output, and what organizational guidance and support they need.
problem: Workplace use carries consequences that personal use may not. An inaccurate output can affect a colleague, client, or organizational record, and employees must make decisions about confidentiality, verification, disclosure, and professional judgment even when formal guidance is incomplete.
questions: For what tasks do employees use generative AI at work?
How is generative AI incorporated into employees' work, and what positive or negative impacts do they experience?
How do employees assess AI-assisted work and verify generated output?
How do organizations support or fail to support employee use?
Why do employees use, selectively use, or avoid generative AI?
How do employees decide whether a particular use is appropriate?
role: I co-designed the study, prepared the GWU IRB materials, conducted interviews with NIST employees, and am co-leading qualitative coding and analysis.
status: 38 interviews completed · coding and analysis underway
collaborators: Conducted with researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).

title: Practitioner Perspectives on Human-Centered AI Evaluation
oneLiner: Interviews with people who design, conduct, support, or use AI evaluations about what human-centered evaluation looks like in practice.
summary: This study asks how practitioners define human-centered AI evaluation, which methods and evidence they use, whose perspectives are included, how disagreement and subjective feedback are handled, and what tools or workflows are missing.
problem: A team can value user perspectives and still face practical questions: whom to recruit, how much evidence is enough, how to interpret conflicting feedback, and how evaluation findings become something a research, product, or governance team can use. This study examines how those choices are made in practice.
questions: How do practitioners define human-centered AI evaluation?
Which methods, criteria, and forms of evidence do they use?
Where does human judgment enter the evaluation process?
Whose perspectives are included, and how is disagreement handled?
Which methodological, organizational, technical, or governance constraints make evaluation difficult?
What tools, documentation, workflows, or data exports are missing?
How are findings interpreted, communicated, and acted upon?
role: I designed the study and interview protocol and obtained GWU IRB approval. Recruitment and interviews are planned as part of my dissertation research.
status: Study and interview protocol complete · GWU IRB approved · recruitment pending

title: Privacy Label Observatory and Ecosystem Studies
oneLiner: Longitudinal measurement, policy comparison, and developer research on how app privacy labels are created and maintained.
summary: This research line tracks Apple privacy labels over time, compares labels with apps' privacy policies, and studies why developers update — or leave unchanged — their disclosures. The public Privacy Label Observatory makes longitudinal privacy-label data available through per-app histories and ecosystem-level views.
problem: Privacy labels are useful only when they continue to reflect an app's data practices. Apps, dependencies, and development teams change, but the disclosure may remain untouched. This work studies where that maintenance process breaks down.
whyItMatters: Across the studies, disclosure problems arise from more than deliberate deception. Developers may not know what third-party components collect, responsibility may be divided across teams, and privacy-label maintenance may sit outside normal development workflows.
role: I built Android crawling infrastructure, contributed to systems for collecting and visualizing longitudinal privacy-label data, and supported privacy-policy and label analysis. I also contributed to the developer-study protocol and early interviews.
scale: 926,240 apps (developer-update study) · 1.6 million apps (longitudinal dataset) · 128 developer survey responses · 19 interviews
